subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's Secret Garden Grid
hook: Priya is designing a square garden in Mumbai to plant herbs. Her friend Arjun wonders why squaring and cubing numbers matters for real life—until a giant terracotta cube planter arrives.

slides.title: Garden Grid Mystery
slides.storyContext: Priya sketches her dream herb garden: a perfect square plot in her Mumbai balcony. 'If each side is 8 meters, how many square meters of soil do I need?' Arjun laughs: 'Just count the tiles!' But there are too many. Priya shows him the shortcut: 8 × 8 = 64 square meters.
slides.inSimpleWords: A square number is a number times itself.

slides.title: Perfect Squares Defined

points.label: Definition
points.text: A perfect square is the product of a number multiplied by itself: n² = n × n

points.label: Visual
points.text: 3² forms a 3×3 grid = 9 unit squares (think chessboard tiles)

slides.inSimpleWords: Perfect squares are numbers that form grids.

slides.title: Example 1: Garden Area

example.problem: Priya's square garden has each side 6 meters. What is the total area?
example.solution: Area = side × side = 6 × 6 = 36 square meters. So 6² = 36.

slides.inSimpleWords: 6 squared equals 36 square meters.

slides.title: The Giant Cube Planter
slides.storyContext: A massive terracotta cube arrives at Priya's building. Arjun opens the manual: 'This cube holds exactly 3 cubic meters of soil. How many unit cubes fit inside?' Priya thinks: 'If each edge is 2 meters... 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cubes!'
slides.inSimpleWords: A cube number is multiplying a number three times.

slides.title: Perfect Cubes Defined

points.label: Definition
points.text: A perfect cube is a number multiplied by itself three times: n³ = n × n × n

points.label: Volume Context
points.text: 3³ = 27 means a 3×3×3 cube holds 27 unit cubes (like sugar cubes stacked)

slides.inSimpleWords: Perfect cubes are numbers that form 3D blocks.

slides.title: Example 2: Terracotta Planter

example.problem: A cubic planter has edges of 4 meters. What volume of soil fits inside?
example.solution: Volume = length × width × height = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cubic meters. So 4³ = 64.

slides.inSimpleWords: 4 cubed equals 64 cubic meters volume.

slides.title: Squares and Cubes

points.text: Perfect squares (n²) are used for area of square plots.
Perfect cubes (n³) are used for volume of cubic containers.
Priya designs gardens, Arjun builds—both use math daily in Mumbai.

slides.inSimpleWords: Squares and cubes help measure space and volume.

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun's Bacteria Lab
hook: Arjun observes bacteria doubling every hour in his school science lab. 2, 4, 8, 16... By day 10, the count is huge. Priya uses exponents to predict it: 2¹⁰ = 1024. How does she do it so fast?

slides.title: Doubling Bacteria Count
slides.storyContext: Arjun's biology class grows bacteria in a petri dish. Day 1: 2 cells. Day 2: 4. Day 3: 8. By day 5, he counts 32 cells. 'But how do I predict day 10 without counting all week?' Priya smiles: 'Use powers. On day 10, you'll have 2 to the power 10.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Exponents are shortcuts for repeated multiplication.

slides.title: Exponent Notation

points.label: Definition
points.text: aⁿ means 'a multiplied by itself n times.' a is the base, n is the exponent or power.

points.label: Reading
points.text: 2³ = 'two to the power three' or 'two cubed' = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8

points.label: Zero Exponent
points.text: Any number to the power 0 equals 1: a⁰ = 1 (e.g., 5⁰ = 1)

slides.inSimpleWords: Exponents show how many times to multiply.

slides.title: Example 1: Bacteria Growth

example.problem: On day 6, Arjun has 2⁶ bacteria. Calculate the count.
example.solution: 2⁶ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 64 bacteria on day 6.

slides.inSimpleWords: 2 to the power 6 is 64 bacteria.

slides.title: Laws of Exponents

points.label: Multiplication Rule
points.text: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ (multiply: add exponents). E.g., 2³ × 2² = 2⁵ = 32

points.label: Division Rule
points.text: aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ (divide: subtract exponents). E.g., 2⁵ ÷ 2² = 2³ = 8

points.label: Power of Power
points.text: (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐˣⁿ (raise to power: multiply exponents). E.g., (2²)³ = 2⁶ = 64

slides.inSimpleWords: Rules make big exponent problems simpler.

slides.title: Example 2: Applying Laws

example.problem: Simplify 3⁴ × 3². Then calculate the result.
example.solution: 3⁴ × 3² = 3⁴⁺² = 3⁶ = 729. Using the multiplication rule saves time.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine exponents using the multiplication rule.

slides.title: Power Play Summary

points.text: Exponents aⁿ replace repeated multiplication.
Laws of exponents simplify big calculations.
Arjun predicts bacteria; Priya predicts using powers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Exponents make patterns and growth easy.

subject: Mathematics
title: Building Mumbai's Community Center
hook: Arjun's uncle is renovating a community center in Mumbai. He needs to choose between square, rectangular, and diamond-shaped plots. Priya explains the angle and side properties. Which shape is sturdiest?

slides.title: Choosing the Plot Shape
slides.storyContext: Arjun's uncle shows three land plots for the community center: one perfectly square, one rectangular, and one diamond-shaped (rhombus). 'Which is strongest?' he asks. Priya pulls out her geometry notes: 'It depends on their angles and sides. All quadrilaterals have 4 sides and angles summing to 360°.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Quadrilaterals are 4-sided closed figures.

slides.title: Angle Sum Property

points.label: Rule
points.text: Sum of all interior angles in any quadrilateral = 360°

points.label: Proof Context
points.text: Divide any quadrilateral into 2 triangles. Each triangle = 180°. Total = 360°.

points.label: Example
points.text: Rectangle: 90° + 90° + 90° + 90° = 360°. Diamond (rhombus): all 4 angles also sum to 360°.

slides.inSimpleWords: All 4 angles in a quadrilateral add to 360°.

slides.title: Example 1: Finding Unknown Angle

example.problem: A quadrilateral has angles 80°, 100°, and 75°. Find the 4th angle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find missing angles using the 360° rule.

slides.title: Types of Quadrilaterals

points.label: Square
points.text: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles (90° each). Most stable for building.

points.label: Rectangle
points.text: Opposite sides equal, 4 right angles. Flexible length-to-width ratio.

points.label: Rhombus (Diamond)
points.text: 4 equal sides but angles NOT all 90°. Angles come in pairs (opposite angles equal).

points.label: Trapezium
points.text: One pair of parallel sides. Most irregular of the common types.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different quadrilaterals have different properties.

slides.title: Example 2: Rhombus Angles

example.problem: A rhombus plot has two angles of 60° each. Find the other two angles.
example.solution: In a rhombus, opposite angles are equal. If 2 angles = 60°, then 60° + 60° + ? + ? = 360°. The other two angles = (360° - 120°) ÷ 2 = 120° each.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rhombus has opposite angles that are equal.

slides.title: Quadrilaterals Overview

points.text: All quadrilaterals have 4 sides and angles summing to 360°.
Squares and rectangles are most stable for construction.
Each type has unique angle and side properties.

slides.inSimpleWords: Quadrilaterals are essential shapes in building.

subject: Mathematics
title: The School Lunch Mystery
hook: The school lunch manager in Delhi needs to divide 144 chapatis equally among students. Priya and Arjun discover divisibility shortcuts: 144 is even (divisible by 2), sums digits to 9 (divisible by 9). How many ways can they divide the chapatis?

slides.title: Dividing Lunch Equally
slides.storyContext: The school has 144 chapatis to serve for lunch. The manager asks: 'Can I divide them equally among 8 students? Among 9? Among 5?' Priya flips through her number tricks notebook: 'Let me check the divisibility rules. 144 ends in 4, so it's even (divisible by 2). Add digits: 1+4+4=9, divisible by 9!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Divisibility rules find factors without dividing.

slides.title: Divisibility Rules

points.label: Divisibility by 2
points.text: Number ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. E.g., 144 ends in 4 → divisible by 2.

points.label: Divisibility by 3
points.text: Sum of digits is divisible by 3. E.g., 144: 1+4+4=9 (divisible by 3) → 144 divisible by 3.

points.label: Divisibility by 9
points.text: Sum of digits is divisible by 9. E.g., 144: 1+4+4=9 → divisible by 9.

points.label: Divisibility by 5
points.text: Number ends in 0 or 5. E.g., 145 ends in 5 → divisible by 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Quick tricks test if numbers divide evenly.

slides.title: Example 1: Chapati Division

example.problem: Check if 144 chapatis can be divided equally among 9 students.
example.solution: Use divisibility by 9: sum of digits = 1+4+4 = 9. Since 9 is divisible by 9, 144 is divisible by 9. Each student gets 144÷9 = 16 chapatis.

slides.inSimpleWords: 144 divided by 9 gives exactly 16 per student.

slides.title: Prime vs. Composite

points.label: Prime Number
points.text: A number with exactly 2 factors: 1 and itself. E.g., 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19 are prime.

points.label: Composite Number
points.text: A number with more than 2 factors. E.g., 4 (factors: 1,2,4), 6 (factors: 1,2,3,6), 144 (many factors).

points.label: 1 is Special
points.text: 1 has only 1 factor (itself), so it's neither prime nor composite.

slides.inSimpleWords: Primes have 2 factors; composites have more.

slides.title: Example 2: Prime Check

example.problem: Is 17 a prime number? List all its factors.
example.solution: Factors of 17: 1 and 17 only. Since it has exactly 2 factors, 17 is prime. (No other number divides 17 evenly.)

slides.inSimpleWords: 17 is prime because only 1 and 17 divide it.

slides.title: Number Play Summary

points.text: Divisibility rules save time without actual division.
Prime numbers have exactly 2 factors; composites have more.
144 chapatis divide equally—Priya solved it with rules.

slides.inSimpleWords: Number tricks reveal hidden factors.

subject: Mathematics
title: Recipe Scaling for a School Festival
hook: Priya's mother makes a kheer (rice pudding) for 4 people using 1 cup rice, 2 cups milk, 3 tbsp ghee. For 20 people at the school festival, how much of each ingredient? Arjun uses ratios to scale the recipe perfectly.

slides.title: Scaling the Festival Kheer
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother's kheer recipe serves 4 people: 1 cup rice, 2 cups milk, 3 tbsp ghee. The school festival expects 20 people. 'Do I just add more randomly?' she asks. Arjun says: 'No! Scale using ratios. The recipe must stay in the same proportion.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Proportions scale recipes and measurements.

slides.title: Ratios Explained

points.label: Definition
points.text: A ratio compares two quantities. Rice : Milk = 1 : 2 means for every 1 cup rice, use 2 cups milk.

points.label: Equivalent Ratios
points.text: 1:2 = 2:4 = 3:6 = 5:10. Multiply or divide both parts by the same number.

points.label: Scaling Factor
points.text: Original 4 people → 20 people: scale factor = 20÷4 = 5. Multiply all ingredients by 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ratios show how quantities relate to each other.

slides.title: Example 1: Scaling Kheer

example.problem: Scale the kheer recipe for 20 people. Original (4 people): 1 cup rice, 2 cups milk, 3 tbsp ghee.
example.solution: Scale factor = 20÷4 = 5. New recipe: 1×5 = 5 cups rice, 2×5 = 10 cups milk, 3×5 = 15 tbsp ghee.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply all ingredients by the scale factor.

slides.title: Direct Proportion

points.label: Definition
points.text: Two quantities are directly proportional if as one increases, the other increases at the same rate.

points.label: Ratio Check
points.text: If x and y are directly proportional, x:y is always the same. E.g., 1 rice : 2 milk stays 5 rice : 10 milk (ratio 1:2 unchanged).

points.label: Formula
points.text: y = kx, where k is the constant of proportionality. E.g., milk = 2 × rice.

slides.inSimpleWords: Directly proportional means equal scaling always.

slides.title: Example 2: Money and Items

example.problem: If 3 notebooks cost Rs 60, what do 7 notebooks cost? (Assuming direct proportion.)
example.solution: Cost per notebook = 60÷3 = Rs 20. Cost of 7 notebooks = 7×20 = Rs 140. Alternatively: 3:60 = 7:x → x = (7×60)÷3 = Rs 140.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cost scales directly with number of items.

slides.title: Proportional Reasoning

points.text: Ratios compare quantities; equivalent ratios stay proportional.
Scaling factor multiplies all ingredients or quantities.
Direct proportion means one quantity drives another at constant rate.

slides.inSimpleWords: Proportions scale recipes and prices perfectly.

subject: Mathematics
title: Cricket Scores and Batting Averages
hook: Arjun watches an Indian cricket match. The batter has a batting average of 0.75 (three hits in four attempts). Is that the same as ¾? Priya shows him how decimals, fractions, and percentages are all the same number dressed up differently.

slides.title: Batting Average Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arjun watches the IPL (Indian Premier League) match on TV. Commentator says: 'Batter's average this season: 0.75.' Arjun wonders: 'Is that good?' Priya says: '0.75 = ¾ = 75%. That means 3 hits out of every 4 attempts. Pretty good for cricket!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Decimals, fractions, and percentages are the same.

slides.title: Fractions to Decimals

points.label: Conversion
points.text: Divide numerator by denominator. E.g., ¾ = 3÷4 = 0.75

points.label: Repeating Decimals
points.text: ⅓ = 0.333... (repeating). ⅙ = 0.1666... (repeating). Write with bar: 0.3̄

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide numerator by denominator to get decimal.

slides.title: Example 1: Cricket Batting Average

example.problem: A cricketer hits 5 fours in 8 deliveries. Express as fraction, decimal, and percentage.
example.solution: Fraction: ⅝. Decimal: 5÷8 = 0.625. Percentage: 0.625 × 100 = 62.5%. All three express the same batting success.

slides.inSimpleWords: ⅝ = 0.625 = 62.5% all mean the same.

slides.title: Decimals to Fractions

points.label: Method
points.text: Write decimal over appropriate power of 10. E.g., 0.75 = 75/100, then simplify to ¾.

points.label: Simplification
points.text: Find GCD of numerator and denominator. E.g., 75/100: GCD=25 → (75÷25)/(100÷25) = ¾

slides.inSimpleWords: Put decimal over 10, 100, 1000 to make fraction.

slides.title: Example 2: Percentage to Fraction

example.problem: Express 40% as a fraction in simplest form.

slides.inSimpleWords: 40% equals two-fifths of the whole.

slides.title: Fractions in Disguise

points.text: Decimals, fractions, and percentages express the same quantity.
Convert by dividing (fraction to decimal) or using powers of 10 (decimal to fraction).
Cricket batting average 0.75 = ¾ = 75%—all the same 'disguised' number.

slides.inSimpleWords: One number, three different disguises.

subject: Science
title: Priya's Organic Farm in Punjab
hook: Priya's grandparents run an organic farm near Amritsar, Punjab. They grow wheat and rice using rotation, composting, and natural pest control. How do crop selection, soil quality, and water management make farming successful?

slides.title: Grandpa's Wheat Field
slides.storyContext: Priya visits the Punjab farm during harvest. Golden wheat fields stretch for acres. 'Grandpa, how do you keep this soil so rich year after year?' Baldev smiles: 'We rotate crops—wheat one year, legumes next. We compost, we let the land rest. The soil is living.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Good farming needs planning, soil care, and rotation.

slides.title: Essential Crop Requirements

points.label: Soil Nutrients
points.text: Crops need Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), Potassium (K). NPK varies by crop type. Wheat needs high N; legumes add N to soil.

points.label: Water Management
points.text: Irrigation timing is critical. Wheat in Punjab: rabi crop (winter); rice: kharif (monsoon). Wrong water = crop failure.

points.label: Sunlight & Temperature
points.text: Wheat thrives in cool season. Rice in warm, monsoon season. Altitude and latitude affect crop choice.

slides.inSimpleWords: Crops need nutrients, water, light, and right temperature.

slides.title: Example 1: Crop Rotation

example.problem: Grandpa grows wheat (high N demand) year 1. What should he grow year 2 to restore nitrogen?
example.solution: Grow legumes (chickpea, peas, clover). They have nitrogen-fixing bacteria in roots that add N to soil. Year 3: wheat again, with richer soil.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rotate wheat and legumes every 2 years.

slides.title: Pest & Weed Control

points.label: Natural Pest Control
points.text: Use ladybugs to eat aphids, neem oil spray, crop rotation to break pest cycles. Avoid pesticides that poison soil.

points.label: Weed Management
points.text: Pull weeds by hand (organic farms). Mulching prevents weed growth. Wrong: herbicides that harm beneficial insects.

points.label: Intercropping
points.text: Plant maize + beans together. Beans climb maize; maize shades soil. Both thrive; pests confused.

slides.inSimpleWords: Natural methods protect crops and soil.

slides.title: Example 2: Neem Spray Application

example.problem: Grandpa notices aphids on wheat. Mix neem oil spray (organic): 2% neem oil in water. Spray at sunrise. How often?
example.solution: Spray every 7-10 days during pest season. Repeat 3-4 times. Natural neem targets aphids without harming bees or soil microbes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Neem spray every 7-10 days controls aphids.

slides.title: Sustainable Farming

points.text: Crop rotation, composting, and natural pest control sustain soil health.
Water, nutrients, sunlight, and temperature must match crop needs.
Grandpa's Punjab farm thrives using age-old organic wisdom.

slides.inSimpleWords: Respect soil, rotate crops, use nature wisely.

subject: Science
title: Arjun's Lab Discoveries
hook: Arjun swabs different surfaces in his Delhi school: bathroom, kitchen, hands before/after washing. Under the microscope, he sees millions of bacteria. Some are helpful (yogurt bacteria). Some cause disease. How do we tell good from bad?

slides.title: Swab Under the Microscope
slides.storyContext: Arjun grows bacteria cultures in petri dishes from different school locations. 'Mrs. Sharma, the bathroom sample has way more colonies than the kitchen!' She nods: 'Bacteria are everywhere—most harmless, some useful, few dangerous. Let's identify them.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Bacteria are tiny single-celled organisms everywhere.

slides.title: Types of Microorganisms

points.label: Bacteria
points.text: Single-celled, no nucleus. Some helpful (gut bacteria aid digestion), some harmful (cause infections). Reproduce by splitting in two.

points.label: Fungi
points.text: Molds, yeasts, mushrooms. Fungi break down dead matter. Some edible (mushrooms), some toxic (food mold).

points.label: Viruses
points.text: Smaller than bacteria, need host cell to replicate. Cause colds, flu, COVID. Not living, but parasitic.

points.label: Protozoa
points.text: Single-celled protists. Some harmful (malaria parasite), some eat bacteria (benefit ecosystems).

slides.inSimpleWords: Bacteria, fungi, and viruses are microorganisms.

slides.title: Example 1: Yogurt Bacteria

example.problem: Yogurt is made from Lactobacillus bacteria. How is this beneficial?
example.solution: Lactobacillus ferments milk sugar (lactose) into lactic acid, curdling milk into yogurt. This bacteria also aids human digestion and boosts immunity. A friendly helper microbe.

slides.inSimpleWords: Yogurt bacteria are helpful friends.

slides.title: Helpful vs. Harmful Microbes

points.label: Helpful Bacteria
points.text: Yogurt (Lactobacillus), gut bacteria (aid digestion), soil bacteria (fix nitrogen for plants), decomposers (break down waste).

points.label: Harmful Bacteria
points.text: Streptococcus (sore throat), E. coli (food poisoning), Salmonella (diarrhea), Tuberculosis (TB).

points.label: Prevention
points.text: Wash hands, clean food, cook properly, get vaccines, boil water, cover mouth when coughing.

slides.inSimpleWords: Good microbes help us; bad ones need prevention.

slides.title: Example 2: Hand Washing Impact

example.problem: Arjun swabs his hands before and after washing. Before: 500 bacterial colonies. After washing with soap: 50 colonies. Why?
example.solution: Soap breaks bacterial cell membranes. Mechanical scrubbing removes bacteria. Hand washing reduces disease risk by ~50%. Essential hygiene habit.

slides.inSimpleWords: Washing removes 90% of harmful bacteria.

slides.title: Microbe Summary

points.text: Bacteria, fungi, and viruses are everywhere.
Some microbes help us (yogurt, gut health, decomposition); others cause disease.
Arjun's lab proves: hygiene and knowledge protect health.

slides.inSimpleWords: Not all microbes are bad—some are essential.

subject: Science
title: Priya's Diwali Diya Experiment
hook: During Diwali celebrations in Delhi, Priya lights dozens of oil diyas (earthen lamps). 'Why does the flame burn?' she wonders. Her science teacher explains: combustion needs three things—fuel, oxygen, and heat. Remove any one, the flame dies.

slides.title: Why Diyas Burn
slides.storyContext: Priya fills oil diyas for Diwali. She lights one, and it glows warmly. 'Why does oil burn? And why does the flame need air?' The teacher says: 'Burn is a chemical reaction. Oil is fuel. It mixes with oxygen in air, and the heat keeps it going.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Burning (combustion) is a chemical reaction.

slides.title: The Combustion Triangle

points.label: Three Requirements
points.text: Fuel (oil, wood, coal, gas), Oxygen (from air), Heat (ignition temperature). All three → fire. Remove one → flame dies.

points.label: Fuel Types
points.text: Combustible materials: oil, wood, coal, petrol, LPG, wax. Each has different ignition temperature.

points.label: Ignition Temperature
points.text: Minimum heat needed to start combustion. Oil ~370°C, wood ~300°C, petrol ~250°C. Above this, fuel burns if oxygen present.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fire needs fuel, oxygen, and heat together.

slides.title: Example 1: Diya Burning

example.problem: A diya burns with oil + cotton wick. Explain why it keeps burning despite cool air outside.
example.solution: Fuel: oil (wick absorbs it). Oxygen: air around flame provides it. Heat: combustion reaction sustains ~600°C at flame. As long as all three are present, diya burns. Wind or water removes oxygen or heat → flame dies.

slides.inSimpleWords: Diya burns because fuel, oxygen, and heat persist.

slides.title: Flame Stages & Safety

points.label: Combustion Reaction
points.text: Fuel + Oxygen → Carbon Dioxide + Water + Energy (heat & light). E.g., oil combustion: C₈H₁₈ + 12O₂ → 8CO₂ + 9H₂O + heat

points.label: Flame Properties
points.text: Blue flame: complete combustion, efficient, cool to watch. Yellow/orange: incomplete combustion, soot produced, less efficient.

points.label: Fire Safety
points.text: Remove fuel (extinguish source), reduce oxygen (smother with blanket), cool flame (water). Never throw water on oil fire—spreads it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Complete combustion (blue) is cleaner and safer.

slides.title: Example 2: Extinguishing a Fire

example.problem: Oil lamp catches fire on the floor. How to extinguish safely?
example.solution: NEVER use water (spreads oil). Instead: smother with blanket to cut oxygen. Or use sand to cool and suffocate flame. Move away and call adults. Oil fire needs oxygen removal, not water.

slides.inSimpleWords: Smother oil fire with blanket, not water.

slides.title: Combustion and Flame

points.text: Combustion = fuel + oxygen + heat. Remove any one → no fire.
Blue flame (complete) vs. yellow flame (incomplete) differ in efficiency.
Priya's Diwali diyas glow safely when combustion is understood.

slides.inSimpleWords: Understanding fire keeps celebrations safe.

subject: Science
title: Arjun's Tiger Reserve Visit
hook: Arjun and his school visit Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve in Madhya Pradesh. A guide explains: only 3,000 tigers remain in India. Habitat loss, poaching, and climate change threaten them. How can communities and laws protect endangered species?

slides.title: Tiger in Danger
slides.storyContext: At Bandhavgarh Reserve, the guide shows Arjun a tiger pug mark (paw print) in mud. 'This tiger roams 50 square kilometers. But forests shrink. Villagers hunt prey. Poachers hunt tigers for pelts. Without protection, tigers vanish in 20 years.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Endangered animals need habitats and protection laws.

slides.title: Causes of Extinction

points.label: Habitat Loss
points.text: Forests cleared for farms, cities, dams. Tigers need unbroken forests to hunt. Fragmented habitat = small populations → extinction risk.

points.label: Poaching & Hunting
points.text: Illegal killing for horns, pelts, meat. Rhinos hunted for horns (used in traditional medicine). Elephants for ivory.

points.label: Climate Change
points.text: Temperature rise, drought, flood affect food chains. Prey species decline → predators starve. Seasons shift → breeding patterns disrupt.

points.label: Pollution
points.text: Pesticides accumulate in food chains. Factory waste poisons rivers. Species sensitive to pollution decline first.

slides.inSimpleWords: Habitat loss, poaching, and climate change threaten species.

slides.title: Example 1: Tiger Population Math

example.problem: India had 10,000 tigers in 1900. By 1970: 1,800. By 2022: 3,700 (through reserves). What happened?
example.solution: 1900-1970: 88% decline (habitat loss, unrestricted hunting). 1970-2022: recovery via Project Tiger (protection laws, reserves, anti-poaching patrols). Shows: laws work, but recovery takes decades.

slides.inSimpleWords: Project Tiger laws brought tigers back from brink.

slides.title: Conservation Strategies

points.label: Protected Areas
points.text: National parks and reserves: legal protection, anti-poaching teams, habitat restoration. Bandhavgarh, Sundarbans (Bengal tigers), Gir (Asiatic lions).

points.label: Wildlife Laws
points.text: India: Wildlife Protection Act 1972. Ban illegal trade. Project Tiger, Project Elephant, Project Rhinoceros. Penalties for poaching.

points.label: Community Involvement
points.text: Train local guides, employ reserve staff from villages. Compensation for livestock lost to predators. Education: villagers become conservationists.

points.label: Captive Breeding
points.text: Breed endangered species in zoos/reserves, reintroduce to wild. Indian rhinoceros (1 left in 1900) → now 3,500 via breeding + protection.

slides.inSimpleWords: Protected reserves, laws, and community action save species.

slides.title: Example 2: Project Tiger Success

example.problem: Project Tiger (launched 1973) protects tigers in 51 reserves across India. How does this save them?
example.solution: Reserves provide continuous forest (habitat). Anti-poaching patrols prevent hunting. Wildlife corridors link reserves so tigers breed freely. Monitoring tracks population. Result: tigers increased from 1,827 (1972) to 3,747 (2022).

slides.inSimpleWords: Project Tiger's reserves, corridors, and patrols work.

slides.title: Conservation Imperative

points.text: Habitat loss, poaching, climate change drive extinction.
Protected reserves, laws, and community involvement restore populations.
Arjun learns: every person can help conserve India's wildlife.

slides.inSimpleWords: Protect habitats, enforce laws, involve communities.

subject: Science
title: Priya's Fish Tank Journey
hook: Priya keeps guppies in a home aquarium in Bangalore. She notices babies appearing. Her guppies reproduce sexually (male + female). Meanwhile, her biology class studies asexual reproducers like starfish and hydra. How do different animals create the next generation?

slides.title: Baby Guppies Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Priya's aquarium suddenly has dozens of tiny guppies. 'I only had 2 adult fish!' she says. Teacher explains: 'Your male and female guppies mated. The female is viviparous—she carries babies inside and gives live birth. Sexual reproduction combines two parents.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Animals reproduce to create offspring for the next generation.

slides.title: Sexual Reproduction

points.label: Definition
points.text: Offspring created from two parents: male + female gametes (sperm + egg). Offspring inherit DNA from both parents, so unique.

points.label: Stages
points.text: Mating → Fertilization (sperm + egg fuse) → Development. Timing varies: guppies (live birth), chickens (eggs), humans (9-month pregnancy).

points.label: Examples
points.text: Guppies, dogs, cats, humans, birds, snakes—most animals reproduce sexually. Variation in offspring → adaptation to environment.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sexual reproduction needs male and female parents.

slides.title: Example 1: Guppy Life Cycle

example.problem: Priya's female guppy is pregnant for 3 weeks. How many babies might she have? (Guppies bear 10-50 live young per cycle.)
example.solution: Gestation: 3 weeks. Birth: 20-30 live guppies (viviparous). Babies grow in 3-4 months to adulthood. Priya's population explodes! (She must control breeding or rehome excess.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Guppies give live birth every 3-4 weeks.

slides.title: Asexual Reproduction

points.label: Definition
points.text: Offspring created from ONE parent only. No gametes. Offspring are genetic clones of parent.

points.label: Methods
points.text: Binary fission (bacteria splits in two), budding (hydra grows bud → detaches as new animal), fragmentation (starfish arm breaks off → regenerates).

points.label: Examples
points.text: Hydra (freshwater), starfish, some flatworms, bacteria, plants (runners, tubers). Advantage: fast population growth. Disadvantage: no variation → less adaptation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Asexual reproduction uses one parent only.

slides.title: Example 2: Hydra Budding

example.problem: Biology class observes hydra under microscope. A bud forms on the side. In 5 days, it detaches as a new hydra. Is this sexual?
example.solution: No—budding is asexual. One parent, no gametes, genetically identical offspring. Hydra (freshwater polyp) reproduces this way when food is plentiful. Sexual reproduction occurs only under stress.

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydra budding is asexual—one parent, clones.

slides.title: Reproduction Summary

points.text: Sexual reproduction (male + female) creates variation; asexual (one parent) creates clones.
Guppies: sexual, live-bearing. Hydra: asexual, budding.
Priya's aquarium shows nature's endless cycle of life.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sexual and asexual—both ways life continues.

subject: Science
title: Arjun's Cricket Ball Physics
hook: Arjun plays cricket at a Delhi park. When he hits the ball hard, it flies far. When he hits softly, it barely rolls. Force applied changes motion. He also notices his cricket spike shoes sink in wet grass while flat shoes don't. Pressure (force per area) explains both.

slides.title: Hard Hit, Far Ball
slides.storyContext: Arjun hits a cricket ball with full force—it soars across the field. 'I hit gently earlier and it barely moved.' Coach explains: 'Force changes motion. Greater force → greater acceleration. Newton's second law: F = ma. More force, more speed.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Force causes changes in motion.

slides.title: What is Force?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Force is a push or pull that changes motion (velocity) or shape. Measured in Newtons (N). Every change in motion requires force.

points.label: Newton's Second Law
points.text: F = ma. Force = mass × acceleration. Larger force → faster acceleration. 1 Newton accelerates 1 kg at 1 m/s².

points.label: Examples
points.text: Bat hitting ball (force), gravity pulling things down (force), friction slowing motion (force), engine pushing car (force).

slides.inSimpleWords: Force is push or pull that changes motion.

slides.title: Example 1: Cricket Ball Force

example.problem: A cricket ball (mass 0.16 kg) is hit by Arjun's bat. The ball's velocity changes from 0 to 30 m/s in 0.02 seconds. Calculate force.
example.solution: Acceleration = (30-0)/0.02 = 1,500 m/s². Force = 0.16 × 1,500 = 240 Newtons. A powerful hit!

slides.inSimpleWords: Force on ball = mass × acceleration.

slides.title: Pressure Explained

points.label: Definition
points.text: Pressure = Force / Area. Same force on small area = high pressure. Same force on large area = low pressure.

points.label: Formula
points.text: P = F/A. Measured in Pascals (Pa) or N/m². Example: 100 N over 0.01 m² = 10,000 Pa.

points.label: Real Life
points.text: Spike shoes: sharp point (small area) → high pressure → sinks in wet grass. Flat shoes: large area → low pressure → stays on surface.

slides.inSimpleWords: Pressure is force spread over area.

slides.title: Example 2: Spike vs. Flat Shoes

example.problem: Arjun weighs 50 kg (490 N force on ground). Spike shoe contact area: 1 cm². Flat shoe: 100 cm². Calculate pressure in each.
example.solution: Spike pressure = 490 N / 0.0001 m² = 4,900,000 Pa (extremely high). Flat pressure = 490 N / 0.01 m² = 49,000 Pa. Spikes sink; flat shoes spread force, stay on surface.

slides.inSimpleWords: Spikes concentrate force; flat shoes spread it.

slides.title: Force and Pressure

points.text: Force (F = ma) changes motion; pressure = force/area concentrates or disperses it.
Hard hit = large force = far ball. Spike shoes = high pressure = sink.
Arjun's cricket game demonstrates physics every day.

slides.inSimpleWords: Force and pressure explain motion and impact.
